# CHAPTER V

BERLIN (1858-1859)

A fourth child has the strength of his weakness. Being of no great value, he may throw himself away if he likes, and never be missed. Charles Francis Adams felt no love for Europe, which, as all the world agreed, unfitted Americans for America—though a captious critic might have replied that all the success he or his father or grandfather achieved was chiefly due to the field Europe gave them. So much more timid are parents for their children than for themselves, that Mr. and Mrs. Adams would have been content to see their children remain forever in Mount Vernon Street, could they have relied on the moral influences of Boston itself. Their dread of vice perhaps worried them less than their dread of sons-in-law or daughters-in-law who might not fit the narrow quarters of home.

The boy Henry wanted to go to Europe; he observed conventions when he could not escape them; his moral principles, if he had any, were not known to be bad. When he presented his request to begin at a German university the study of the Civil Law—although neither he nor his exceedingly indulgent parents knew what the Civil Law was, or any reason for his studying it—they dutifully consented, and walked with him down to the railway-station at Quincy to bid him good-bye, with a smile which he almost thought a tear.

He sailed on the Persia in November, 1858. On the third day the world ran into a heavy storm. He learned then a lesson that stood by him better than any university teaching ever did—the meaning of a November gale on the mid-Atlantic—which, for mere physical misery, passed endurance. One began at last to see that a great many impressions were needed to make very little education, but how many could be crowded into one day without making any education at all, became the pons asinorum of tourist mathematics.

The Persia vanished one Sunday morning in a furious gale in the Mersey, to make place for the drearier picture of a Liverpool street in November murk, followed instantly by the passionate delights of Chester and red-sandstone romance. In days before tourists, when romance was a reality, not a picture, the emotions were overwhelming. At Eaton Hall, the boys were awed as Thackeray or Dickens would have felt in the presence of a Duke. The very name of Grosvenor struck a note of grandeur. The lofty gilded rooms, the portraits, the gardens, the sense of superiority in the England of the fifties, set the rich nobleman apart, above Americans and shopkeepers. Aristocracy was real. So was the England of Dickens. Oliver Twist and Little Nell lurked in every churchyard shadow, not as shadow but alive. Even Charles the First was not very shadowy, standing on the tower to see his army defeated.

Then came the journey up to London through Birmingham and the Black District. The plunge into darkness lurid with flames; the sense of unknown horror in this weird gloom which then existed nowhere else, and never had existed before, except in volcanic craters; the violent contrast between this dense, smoky, impenetrable darkness and the soft green charm one glided into as one emerged—the revelation of an unknown society of the pit—made a boy uncomfortable, though he had no idea that Karl Marx was standing there waiting for him, and that sooner or later the process of education would have to deal with Karl Marx much more than with Professor Bowen of Harvard or his Satanic free-trade majesty John Stuart Mill.

London was still London. A certain style dignified its grime; heavy, clumsy, arrogant, purse-proud, but not cheap; insular but large; barely tolerant of an outside world, and absolutely self-confident. No stranger had rights even in the Strand. The eighteenth century held its own. History muttered down Fleet Street, like Dr. Johnson, in Adams's ear; Vanity Fair was alive on Piccadilly in yellow chariots with coachmen in wigs; half the great houses, black with London smoke, bore large funereal hatchments; the most insolent structures in the world were the Royal Exchange and the Bank of England. In November, 1858, London was still vast, but it was the London of the eighteenth century that an American felt and hated.

Education went backward. The next step took it back to the sixteenth. He crossed to Antwerp. As the Baron Osy steamed up the Scheldt in the morning mists, a travelling band on deck began to play, and peasants in the fields dropped their tools to join in dancing. Ostade and Teniers were as much alive as they ever were, and even the Duke of Alva was still at home. The thirteenth-century cathedral towered above a sixteenth-century mass of tiled roofs. The taste of the town was thick, rich, ripe, like a sweet wine; but he might as well have drunk out his excitement in old Malmsey, for all the education he got from it. He never dreamed of trying to educate himself to the Descent from the Cross. He was only too happy to feel himself kneeling at the foot of it; he learned only to loathe the sordid necessity of getting up again.

Dropped into Berlin one morning without guide or direction, the young man in search of education floundered in a mere mess of misunderstandings. A student at twenty takes easily to anything, and he would have accepted the thirteenth century pure and simple since his guides assured him this was his right path; but a week's experience left him dazed and dull. Within a day or two he was running about to beer-cellars and music-halls, smoking bad tobacco, drinking poor beer, eating sauerkraut and sausages. One can always descend the social ladder. The trouble came when he asked for the education he was promised. His friends took him to be registered at the university, selected his professors and courses, showed him where to buy the Institutes of Gaius and several German works on the Civil Law, and led him to his first lecture.

What Berlin's Gymnasium and university failed to teach, an accidental afternoon in a beer-hall did: amid stale tobacco and Hausfrauen knitting, Beethoven's symphonic line stole into Adams's unconscious and opened a sense he had not known he possessed, even as the German drill on memory taught him its hard limits.
